content: Ertapenem is a carbapenem-type antibiotic used to treat and prevent a variety of bacterial infections. It is administered either intravenously (IV) or intramuscularly (IM) at a dose of 1 gram per day for up to 14 days. After at least three days of parenteral therapy, patients showing clinical improvement may transition to an appropriate oral (PO) regimen. For diabetic foot infections, treatment may extend up to four weeks depending on the severity of the infection and the patient’s response to therapy, excluding cases involving osteomyelitis. In pediatric patients aged 3 months to 12 years, the recommended dose is 15 mg/kg IV or IM every 12 hours for up to 14 days, not exceeding 1 gram per dose. For children under 3 months, the safety and efficacy of ertapenem have not been established. For patients older than 12 years, the standard adult dose of 1 gram per day IV or IM applies. Ertapenem interacts with several medications and vaccines. It reduces the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG, cholera, and typhoid vaccines, due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is complete. Additionally, ertapenem may decrease the effectiveness of oral microbiota products, certain vitamins (e.g., biotin, thiamine, pyridoxine, and pantothenic acid), and oral contraceptives by altering intestinal flora. Patients using oral contraceptives should consider alternative or additional forms of birth control during treatment. Ertapenem also decreases valproic acid levels, increasing the risk of seizures, and should be avoided or replaced with an alternative drug in such cases. Probenecid increases ertapenem levels by reducing its elimination, though the clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. Ertapenem is contraindicated in patients with known allergies to carbapenems, penicillins, cephalosporins, or lidocaine (if used for IM administration). It should be used cautiously in patients with renal impairment, as dose adjustments are necessary to reduce the risk of seizures. Prolonged use of ertapenem increases the risk of superinfections, including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, which may occur during or after treatment. Long-term or repeated use may also lead to oral thrush or yeast infections. Ertapenem is present in human breast milk, but its effects on breastfed infants and milk production are unknown. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the medication and potential risks to the infant. Data on ertapenem use during pregnancy are limited, and its safety regarding birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes is not well established. Ertapenem should not be co-infused with other medications or diluted with dextrose solutions. Reconstituted IV solutions should be stored at room temperature and used within six hours or refrigerated for up to 24 hours, with an additional four hours allowed at room temperature after removal from refrigeration. IM preparations should be administered into a large muscle mass, such as the gluteal muscle or lateral thigh, and should not be used if the patient has a lidocaine allergy. Common side effects include swelling, redness, pain, or soreness at the injection site, as well as gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and headache. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of all medications, supplements, and allergies before starting ertapenem. Regular monitoring of kidney function and blood counts may be necessary during treatment. In case of a missed dose, patients should contact their healthcare provider for guidance. Proper storage and disposal of the medication are essential, and expired or unused products should be discarded appropriately.
